 The film in which Raavan is the hero rather than the villain
 Mani Ratnam’s ‘Raavanan’ reworks the Ramayana’s narrative arc.
 Nandini Ramnath

 Vikram and Aishwarya Rai Bachchan in Raavanan (2010)
 |
 Madras Talkies
 Some of the box office success of Ramayana: Part 1 can safely be attributed to its characterisation of Raavan, played by Yash. Nitesh Tiwari’s visual effects-heavy film stars Ranbir Kapoor as Ram and Sai Pallavi as Sita. But it is Yash, as a ripped and raging Raavan, who steals the show from the saintly leads.
 Ramayana: Part 1 gives Raavan’s back story as much importance as Ram’s formative years. Most faithful adaptations of the Ramayana epic have always been mindful of Raavan’s exalted status.
 In Ramanand Sagar’s popular television serial Ramayan , the Lankan ruler who triggers a war with Ram after abducting Sita gets a proper farewell. In the episode about Raavan’s defeat and demise, the lyrics of a dirge observe that the wise king was laid low by his hubris.
 Raavan has always been a colourful character. The animated Japanese-Indian film Ramayana: The Legend of Prince Rama (1993), directed by Ram Mohan, Yugo Sako and Koichi Sasaki, imagines Raavan with vampiric teeth and grey whiskers, ruling over a palace crawling with lizards and packed with occupants who resemble monsters.
 Ramayana: The Legend of Prince Rama (1993). Courtesy TEM. In Mani Ratnam’s Raavanan (2010), the villain is the hero.
 Ratnam has dipped into Indian epics and mythology in several of his films. The crime drama Thalapathi (1991) stars Rajinikanth as a contemporary version of Karna from the Mahabharata. Roja , (1992), about a cryptographer kidnapped by Kashmiri militants, reworks the Savitri and Satyavan episode. Raavanan imagines Raavan as a modern-day rebel against police atrocities.
 Raavanan was simultaneously made in both Tamil and Hindi, like Ratnam’s Aayutha Ezhutha (2004), which was released in Hindi as Yuva . While Aayutha Ezhutha and Yuva had entirely different sets of actors, Raavanan/Raavan share Aishwarya Rai Bachchan as the Sita-like Ragini and Vikram.
 Mani Ratnam’s dual-language films have characters standing in for nearly every one of the Ramayana’s major players. In Raavanan , Veera (Vikram) is a fugitive revolutionary; his Lanka a forest with a waterfall. Ram is Dev (Prithviraj Sukumaran), a Superintendent of Police who represents the moral order – and everything that is wrong with it. (In the Hindi version, Vikram plays Dev while Abhishek Bachchan is Raavan).
 Veera’s kidnapping of Dev’s wife Ragini is an extreme act of provocation. There is now a personal element to Dev’s campaign to smash Veera’s parallel government.
 Ragini’s reckless attempt to flee her abduction makes Veera fall in love with her. Initially terrified of Veera, Ragini learns that Veera’s war is personal too.
 His step-sister Vennila (Priyamani) was hauled off to a police station by Dev’s trusted deputy officer and gang-raped there. Raavanan boldly re-frames the slicing of Surpanakha’s nose in the Ramayana as an act of brutal sexual assault. Vennila’s fate tips Veera over the edge.
 Play 
 Usure Pogudhey, Raavanan (2010). While Raavan can be rented from various streaming platforms, including Prime Video and Apple TV, Raavanan is available only on YouTube, that too in Tamil and without subtitles. Raavanan is far superior to the Hindi production, in the main because of Vikram’s mesmerising performance and the setting, which makes more sense in Tamil than in Hindi.
 Abhishek Bachchan isn’t a patch on his counterpart, actively mugging his way through the dramatic moments. Sadly for Abhishek Bachchan, Vikram is effective in the Hindi version too.
 Raavanan is choppily assembled and overwrought at times, overdoing the Veera equals Raavan parallels. Yet, the film’s radical approach to a venerated epic is riveting, and brave.
 Raavanan muddies received wisdom about heroism and villainy, divinity and humanity, justice and punishment. Like Indonesian director Garin Nugroho’s contemporary musical Opera Jawa , Raavanan presents alternate readings of key moments in the Ramayana – the treatment of Surpanakha, Ram’s suspicion over Sita’s virtue, Raavan’s story arc.
 One of the most striking passages in Raavanan is an erotic dream sequence in which Ragini tries to escape from Veera, only to be pursued by him. Staged as a dance that is choreographed by Astad Deboo, the dream is ambiguous about the identity of the dreamer.
 Aishwarya Rai Bachchan in Raavanan (2010). The longer Ragini stays with Veera, the greater her empathy towards him. Raavan is depicted as a rugged romantic, with perfect hand-eye co-ordination in the superb songs by AR Rahman. Ragini is forced to concede that her beloved spouse and his police force have contributed to her plight.
 Ragini’s conflicted feelings for Veera peak in a sequence that is impossible in the polarised, intolerant present. A conversation between Veera and Ragini is both romantic proposal and ethical debate.
 Dev is god-like, a wavering Ragini says. Is that so, Veera sneers – is he god-like or God himself? Is he an “avatara purusha”, an ideal man? Dev’s subsequent behaviour confirms Veera’s skepticism.
 The censor board was decidedly more liberal in 2010. Mani Ratnam got away with an adaptation of the Ramayana that doubted Ram’s righteousness and Raavan’s monstrosity while also rooting itself in social concerns about human right violations and police excesses. Raavanan confirms that the Ramayana is robust enough for interpretation and critique.
 Play 
 Kodu Potta, Raavanan (2010). Tucked into Ratnam’s film is the notion, again borrowed from classic literature, of a woman being the cause of a warrior’s downfall. In the Ramayana, Raavan makes away with Sita as a riposte to Surpanakha’s humiliation – a misjudgment that leads to his death. In Raavanan , Veera wants to avenge Vennila, but his passion for Ragini comes in the way.
 Perhaps unsurprisingly, Raavanan outstripped Raavan at the box office, finding a ready audience in the South for its audacious take on the good-versus-evil paradox. Ratnam’s dark and violent film is decisive about who the narrative’s real hero is. Raavan’s hold over the imagination endures into the latest iteration, which finds itself unable to sidestep the Lankan ruler’s version of events.
